claims.claim: Basdeo reports that after her introductory chapter Larrington adopts the persona of a travel writer for her region-by-region chapters.
claims.source: Stephen Basdeo, review, Medievally Speaking (2016), describing Carolyne Larrington's method
claims.quote: Larrington adopts the persona of a travel writer
claims.page: review body, on the book's structure

claims.claim: Basdeo quotes Larrington that before surnames a patronymic was the only way to distinguish someone from others bearing the same given name.
claims.source: Carolyne Larrington, Winter is Coming (2016) pp.14-15, quoted in Stephen Basdeo's review, Medievally Speaking
claims.quote: a patronymic was the only way to distinguish someone from others

claims.claim: Basdeo reports Larrington's argument that Ned Stark's dominion over Winterfell resembles that of an Anglo-Saxon earl rather than later medieval kingship.
claims.source: Stephen Basdeo, review, Medievally Speaking (2016), reporting Carolyne Larrington p.57
claims.quote: the dominion that an Anglo-Saxon Earl had over his people

claims.claim: Routledge's listing gives Young's third chapter the title 'Look with Your Eyes - Immersion and Thinning'.
claims.source: Routledge publisher listing for Young, George R.R. Martin and the Fantasy Form

claims.claim: Voice's conference abstract states that the first four books of A Song of Ice and Fire were rendered searchable in their entirety for corpus analysis.
claims.source: Matthew Voice, University of Sheffield, Nine Worlds 2014 conference abstract
claims.quote: the first four books of ASOIAF are rendered searchable in their entirety

claims.claim: Acree writes that Maester Yandel, the narrator of The World of Ice and Fire, has presented a history that is undeniably distorted.
claims.source: Cat Acree, BookPage interview feature, December 2014
claims.quote: has presented a history that is undeniably distorted

claims.claim: Acree writes that where Tolkien was concerned with myth and languages, Martin is fascinated by history and the challenges of retelling it.
claims.source: Cat Acree, BookPage interview feature, December 2014

claims.claim: Acree reports that García and Antonsson pored over 10,000 pages of novels, pulling out all references to history, myths and legends, before Martin filled in the blanks.
claims.source: Cat Acree, BookPage interview feature, December 2014
claims.quote: pored over 10,000 pages of novels, pulling out all references to history

claims.claim: Martin told BookPage that he did not want to get too close to the so-called present day of Westeros in the companion history.
claims.source: George R. R. Martin, interviewed by Cat Acree, BookPage, December 2014
claims.quote: too close to the so-called present day of Westeros

claims.claim: Vineyard reports that The World of Ice and Fire is written from the viewpoint of a maester at the Citadel.
claims.quote: written from the viewpoint of a maester at the Citadel

claims.claim: Vineyard reports that the maester's knowledge in The World of Ice and Fire comes from other scrolls that may themselves be unreliable.
claims.quote: comes from other scrolls that, in turn, may be unreliable

claims.claim: Martin told Vulture that people do know things, but the things they know may not be right.
claims.source: George R. R. Martin, interviewed by Jennifer Vineyard, Vulture / Slate, 7 November 2014
claims.quote: the things they ‘know’ may not be right

claims.claim: Martin told Vulture he was supposed to write 50,000 words of text for sidebars and wrote 300,000 instead.
claims.source: George R. R. Martin, interviewed by Jennifer Vineyard, Vulture / Slate, 7 November 2014
claims.quote: I was supposed to write 50,000 words of text for sidebars

claims.claim: Germani describes Martin as setting his narrative atop an iceberg of history and using that background to give the text solidity.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'Now, As We All Know', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: setting your narrative atop this iceberg of history

claims.feature: other: prior life of the cast
claims.claim: Germani writes that part of why Martin's world feels lived-in is that everyone had a life before page one.
claims.source: Erik Germani, 'Now, As We All Know', At Sea Journal
claims.quote: Everyone had a life before page one
